newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Azerbaijan slams Armenia over separatist premier.
newsitem.headline: Azerbaijan slams Armenia over separatist premier.

text.p: Azeri President Heydar Aliyev on Tuesday sharply criticised the appointment of a separatist leader from Azerbaijan's breakaway Nagorno-Karabakh enclave as prime minister of neighbouring Armenia.
"This does not correspond to norms and international laws. We cannot accept such an appointment," he told reporters during a visit to the Ukrainian capital, Kiev.

"We view the appointment of the leader of Karabakh's Armenian community, Robert Kocharyan, as Armenian Prime Minister as negative. We do not understand it because Nagorno-Karabakh is part of Azerbaijan."
But Kocharyan himself, speaking earlier in the Armenian capital Yerevan, told reporters: "I don't think this (my appointment) will have any effect on the Karabakh question."

Nagorno-Karabakh, entirely within Moslem Azerbaijan's borders but populated mostly by Christian ethnic Armenians, broke away from Baku's rule in the late 1980s. Thousands were killed in fighting before a ceasefire was declared three years ago.

"Armenian forces occupied Nagorno-Karabakh and some Azeri territories around it," Aliyev said. "Kocharyan, as so-called president of the self-proclaimed Nagorno-Karabakh Republic, played an active role in this occupation and in a bloody war."
Kocharyan was named to the post last week by Armenian President Levon Ter-Petrosyan in a surprise move.

Diplomats and observers have interpreted Kocharyan's appointment as a hardening of Armenia's stance on the nine-year dispute, the oldest ethnic conflict in the former Soviet Union and one which hastened the demise of Moscow's former empire.

Azeri Foreign Minister Gasan Gasanov told reporters in Kiev that Baku wanted to raise the issue of the supply of Russian tanks to Armenia at a meeting of foreign ministers of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) in Moscow on Thursday.
Officials in the Azeri delegation told Reuters Aliyev would meet Ter-Petrosyan in Moscow on Friday after the summit of former Soviet republics.
Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma and Aliyev denied Armenian allegations that Ukrainian tanks had been supplied to Baku.

Kuchma and Aliyev, whose countries consider each other "strategic partners", said that the CIS should be based on an equal relationship, indicating irritation among some former Soviet republics of Moscow's domination of the 12-member body.
Ukraine, with an eye to diversifying its oil supplies away from Moscow, is trying to prepare the ground for supplies from Azerbaijan's off-shore reserves.
Ukraine, Azerbaijan and Georgia have started setting up a Euro-Asian transport corridor which would allow oil deliveries from Baku to Georgia's Black Sea coast and from there to Ukrainian ports.
Baku makes no secret of plans to use revenues from huge, untapped offshore Caspian Sea reserves to build a military machine able to take back lost lands if peace talks fail.
Gasanov told reporters Baku wanted Kiev to send peacekeepers to Nagorno-Karabakh once a political solution was found.
